vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-H.1(vi) and rules 25-G.2 to 25-G.4, read with BNSS s.404 (formerly CrPC s.363); the same-day handover practice described firsthand by a judgment writer at the Panchkula district courts (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

vocabulary.gloss: The monthly assurance a court official signs and sends to the main office of the establishment, stating that for the preceding month all the orders and judgments have been uploaded. It is a single printed format carrying no case numbers and no counts, only the blanket statement, and at Panchkula it goes down around the third of the month. No rule in the corpus creates it; it belongs to the e-Courts era and sits alongside the older periodical statements Volume III requires - the monthly statement of criminal cases pending over a year, and the monthly statement of summary cases received and disposed of. CIS already reports which orders are still pending upload, which is the report the writer runs for himself before signing.
vocabulary.source: District court reporting practice, Panchkula, described firsthand by a judgment writer (PUCAR interview, June 2026). No provision in this corpus prescribes it; its rule-level ancestors are Rules and Orders Volume III rules 1-A.12 and 2.6.

vocabulary.gloss: The magistrate on the duty roster, before whom work is put up that cannot wait for the court it belongs to. The month is divided among the judges of the establishment in blocks of a few days each, and whatever arises for a court that is on leave goes to whoever holds duty - police remands, bail applications and miscellaneous applications. It is a court-administration arrangement created by no rule in this corpus, but the work it brings is governed: Volume III requires the reasons for a remand to police custody to be recorded and a copy sent to the District Magistrate, and BNSS s.187 is the live custody provision. None of it is cheque-case work; it reaches the s.138 court's staff through the roster, not the case type.
vocabulary.source: District court duty roster, Panchkula, described firsthand by a judgment writer (PUCAR interview, June 2026). No rule in this corpus creates the roster; the remand duty it carries is in Rules and Orders Volume III rule 11-B.9, read with BNSS s.187.

vocabulary.gloss: Signing a judgment or order inside CIS with a digital signature held on a pen-drive token, so that it can be uploaded as a signed document. Orders can be signed and uploaded in a batch, but each one still has to be selected individually, and there is no bulk download. The obligation behind it is old: Volume III r.1-H.1(ii) and (iii) and BNSS s.392(3) require the judgment to be dated and signed by the presiding officer, and every page of it where it was not written in his own hand; IT Act s.5 and s.6 give an electronic signature the same legal effect and authorise its use by courts and government. This is not the same as the digital signature or Aadhaar-based e-Sign the E-Filing Rules require of a party or advocate on an e-filed document.
vocabulary.source: CIS judgment and order workflow, described firsthand by a judgment writer at the Panchkula district courts (PUCAR interview, June 2026); the signature requirement it satisfies is in Rules and Orders Volume III rule 1-H.1 and BNSS s.392, and its legal effect in IT Act sections 5 and 6

institutions.summary: The police and the courts a s.138 case runs through in Haryana - the police grounded in the Haryana Police Act, 2007, the courts in the Constitution and the BNSS. The Punjab and Haryana High Court's rules of practice for the criminal courts are now in the corpus under State rules, as Volume III of its Rules and Orders.

police.summary: The Haryana Police, constituted under the Haryana Police Act, 2007. The force is organised into ranges, police districts and stations; the senior ranks are Indian Police Service (IPS) officers, the rest the Haryana Police Service. A s.138 case rarely involves the police (it is a complaint, not an FIR case).

judiciary.summary: The court hierarchy a s.138 case moves through in Haryana - the trial court is the Judicial Magistrate of the First Class; appeal to the Court of Session; revision and quashing to the Punjab and Haryana High Court; and, by special leave, to the Supreme Court. How each of those courts must run the case is set by the High Court's Rules and Orders, Volume III, under State rules.

roles.entry: Ministerial cadre of the Haryana district judiciary.

story.summary: How a §138 cheque-bounce case runs in Kerala, from filing to disposal - built purely from the rules and Acts, with every step citing the provision that governs it. Click any citation to open the exact text. This is the de jure process the black-letter rules prescribe; the lived, local practice is a separate layer.

roles.who: The payee or the holder in due course of the dishonoured cheque. Only this person can set a §138 case going, by filing the complaint in their own name.

Where duly authorised and personally aware of the transaction, may file the complaint and depose on the complainant's behalf - a point the Supreme Court has settled for §138 cases. Stands in the payee's place, not as a separate party.
The drawer of the cheque, prosecuted for the dishonour. Where the drawer is a company, the company and every person who was in charge of and responsible to it.
Stands surety for the accused's release on bail, undertaking by bond to secure their appearance. The court tests the surety's sufficiency before accepting the bond.
The bank on which the cheque is drawn. Its return of the cheque unpaid is the event the offence turns on, and its return memo proves both the dishonour and the reason for it.
Gives evidence on the facts. In a §138 case the complainant's evidence may be led on affidavit, and an officer of the drawee bank often proves the dishonour. A witness is sworn before deposing.
The legal practitioner who appears for the complainant or the accused. The right to appear flows from enrolment under the Advocates Act.
Assists the advocate with filing, inspection of records and following the matter through the registry. A recognised court-precinct role rather than a statutory office.
roles.basis: Court-precinct and registry practice, governed by the High Court's rules rather than a provision of the substantive law.

roles.who: The Judicial Magistrate of the First Class who takes cognizance of the complaint, tries it summarily and passes judgment. In Kerala a §138 case may be assigned to the designated Special Court.
The court's senior ministerial officer who signs and issues the summons and other process 'by order of the Court'.
The clerk who attends the sitting: calls the cases, marks the exhibits, and keeps the court diary and the proceedings paper - the running record of each hearing.
Takes down the dictation of the depositions, orders and judgment. The depositions they record are headed and signed in the form the rules prescribe.

Interprets the evidence when a witness does not speak the court's language, which matters in Kerala where the court language is Malayalam. The interpreter is put on oath, and a police officer may not interpret the evidence.
The local police officer who executes warrants and serves the process the court issues, as part of the statutory functions of the police.

The court official (part of the Registry / ministerial establishment) who scrutinises a complaint and its documents for defects before it is numbered and placed for cognizance, noting objections or returning it for amendment.

informal.title: 'Scrutiny officer' is the functional name used on the ground; the rules assign scrutiny to 'the Registry' (E-Filing Rules r.17) and returns to the 'officer concerned' (CRP r.68).
informal.practice: Reported (Mehul, PUCAR; unverified): defects are sometimes not marked properly and files held so the advocate approaches the officer and may pay to move the file forward.

steps: A cheque-bounce case is a complaint case: the payee or holder in due course files a written complaint, and the Magistrate can take cognizance only on such a complaint (never on a police report).
It must be filed within one month of the cause of action - which arises when the drawer fails to pay within 15 days of the demand notice served after dishonour.
In Kerala the complaint is e-filed through the DCMS portal under the E-Filing Rules, and the court fee is paid on filing.

Before the complaint is numbered and placed for cognizance it is scrutinised for defects. On e-filing the Registry scrutinises the pleadings and documents and notes objections; a defective petition is not numbered and is returned to the party, pleader or officer concerned for amendment and representation.

On the ground this is done by an official commonly called the scrutiny officer. Reported (Mehul, PUCAR; unverified): defects are sometimes not marked properly and files held so the advocate approaches the officer and may pay to move the file forward. The scrutiny function is in the rules; the title and this practice are not.
The Magistrate examines the complainant (and any witnesses) on oath and, if satisfied there is ground to proceed, takes cognizance and issues process to the accused.
The summons is signed and issued by the court's ministerial officer 'by order of the Court', in the prescribed form.
Because the court language is Malayalam, process issued in Malayalam must carry an authorised English translation.
The summons is served in the manner the BNSS prescribes, and the NI Act's own mode of service also applies.
Service is effected through the police - the local Station House Officer serves the court's process. This is the only point at which the police enter a §138 case.
Where the e-filing regime permits, service may be by electronic means.

process.stage: 4 · If the accused does not appear
steps: The court escalates up the warrant ladder: a warrant issues, and on continued absconding, proclamation and attachment of property.
Kerala's rules carry the absconding-accused track; the police execute the warrant.
The case is tried summarily, and the complainant's evidence may be given on affidavit - the features that make §138 a fast-track offence.
A presumption operates in favour of the holder that the cheque was issued for a debt or liability, unless the accused rebuts it.
Kerala adds nothing procedural here - the summary-trial machinery is uniform central law.
On conviction the court may impose imprisonment up to two years and/or a fine up to twice the cheque amount, with compensation to the complainant.
The offence is compoundable: the parties may settle at any stage and the case is compounded, ending the prosecution.
The accused may appeal; the appellate court may require a deposit of a minimum of 20% of the fine/compensation as a condition of the appeal.
A revision lies to the High Court, whose own rules govern its criminal side.
A complaint may also be challenged by a quashing petition before the High Court.

vocabulary.gloss: The court officer who, 'by order of the Court', ordinarily signs and issues the summons to the accused and witnesses in a Kerala criminal court.
vocabulary.source: Criminal Rules of Practice, Rule 7

vocabulary.gloss: The prescribed words that must precede the ministerial officer's signature on a summons.
vocabulary.source: Criminal Rules of Practice, Rule 7

vocabulary.gloss: The court's running administrative record of a case (Administrative Form No. 10).
vocabulary.source: Criminal Rules of Practice, Rule 72

vocabulary.gloss: The sheet on which the day-to-day proceedings of a case are recorded (Judicial Form No. 61).
vocabulary.source: Criminal Rules of Practice, Rule 73

vocabulary.gloss: The officer in charge of a police station; in a s.138 case the person who executes the court's warrant and serves its process - the only point at which the police enter the case.
vocabulary.source: Kerala Police Act, §4 (functions of the police)
aka: officer in charge of the police station

vocabulary.gloss: The statutory duties of the Kerala police, including serving court process and executing warrants - a s.138 case is a complaint case, so the police act only on the court's process, never by investigation.
vocabulary.source: Kerala Police Act, §4

vocabulary.gloss: Court process issued in Malayalam must carry an authorised English translation - the point where the court-language rule bites on a summons or notice.
vocabulary.source: Criminal Rules of Practice, Rule 14

vocabulary.gloss: The working language of Kerala's subordinate courts; it shapes the summons, the demand-notice evidence, orders and the filing interface a s.138 case passes through.
vocabulary.source: Criminal Rules of Practice, Rule 14

vocabulary.gloss: The District Court Case Management System at filing.keralacourts.in through which a s.138 complaint is electronically filed in Kerala.
vocabulary.source: Electronic Filing Rules (Kerala), 2021, Rule 1

vocabulary.gloss: When the Kerala e-filing regime permits service by electronic means - narrower than informal WhatsApp/e-mail service, which the High Court has declined to sanction (Anoop Jacob).
vocabulary.source: Electronic Filing Rules (Kerala), 2021, Rule 11

vocabulary.gloss: Kollam's dedicated §138 court, running round-the-clock as India's first fully digital 'ON Court' - the concrete court the Kerala layer describes.
A Judicial Magistrate of the First Class court set up under the proviso to section 9(1) BNSS to try only cheque-bounce cases - Kerala's sits at Kollam.

The ad valorem fee to file a cheque complaint in Kerala - ₹250 up to a ₹10,000 cheque, otherwise 5% of the cheque amount capped at ₹3 lakh (Article 21, Court Fees Act; revised by the Finance Act 2025).
vocabulary.source: Kerala Court Fees Act, Article 21

vocabulary.gloss: The clerk who attends the sitting - calls the cases, marks the exhibits, and keeps the court diary and the proceedings paper.
vocabulary.source: Criminal Rules of Practice, Rules 72, 73 & 62

vocabulary.gloss: Takes down the dictation of the depositions, orders and judgment; the depositions are headed and signed as the rules prescribe.
vocabulary.source: Criminal Rules of Practice, Rules 56 & 57

vocabulary.gloss: Interprets the evidence when a witness does not speak the court's language, which in Kerala is Malayalam; put on oath, and a police officer may not interpret.
vocabulary.source: Criminal Rules of Practice, Rules 52 & 54

vocabulary.gloss: A person who stands surety for the accused's release on bail, undertaking by bond to secure their appearance; the court tests the surety's sufficiency.
vocabulary.source: Criminal Rules of Practice, Rules 122 & 124

vocabulary.gloss: Assists the advocate with filing, inspection of records and following the matter through the registry - a recognised court-precinct role rather than a statutory office.
vocabulary.source: Court-precinct and registry practice (not a statutory office)

vocabulary.gloss: How the national Oaths Act, 1969 requirement is run on the ground in Kerala: the Criminal Rules of Practice name the officer who administers the oath (Rule 50) and prescribe its form (Rule 51). A witness, interpreter or deponent is bound by it before giving evidence; one who objects to being sworn makes a solemn affirmation instead.
vocabulary.source: Criminal Rules of Practice, Rules 50 & 51

vocabulary.gloss: The document by which a party authorises an advocate to appear and act for them; until it is on record the advocate has no authority to represent the party. The Kerala Criminal Rules of Practice prescribe its form and attestation (Rule 32).
vocabulary.source: Criminal Rules of Practice, Rule 32

vocabulary.gloss: A witness's evidence as recorded in court and signed. The Kerala Criminal Rules of Practice prescribe how depositions are headed (Rule 56) and signed (Rule 57); in a summary §138 trial much of the evidence reaches the record as affidavits rather than long oral depositions.
vocabulary.source: Criminal Rules of Practice, Rules 56 & 57

vocabulary.gloss: The rules the High Court of Kerala made in 1982, under Article 227 of the Constitution, to govern how the criminal courts below it actually run - filing, the court diary, oaths, depositions, the vakalatnama, bail and so on. This site cites them as the source of most of the Kerala state-layer vocabulary.
vocabulary.source: Criminal Rules of Practice, Kerala, 1982

vocabulary.gloss: The court official (part of the Registry / ministerial establishment) who scrutinises a complaint and its documents for defects before it is numbered and placed for cognizance. On e-filing the Registry scrutinises and notes objections (E-Filing Rules r.17); a defective petition is not numbered and is returned for amendment and representation (CRP r.68). 'Scrutiny officer' is the functional name used on the ground; the rules name 'the Registry' or the 'officer concerned', not this title.
vocabulary.source: E-Filing Rules, Kerala, r.17 (read with CRP r.68)

vocabulary.gloss: The court's administrative office - the ministerial establishment that receives filings, scrutinises them for defects, numbers and lists the case, keeps the records and issues process. A s.138 complaint is presented here before it reaches the Magistrate: the office checks the form and enclosures under the Criminal Rules of Practice (rule 27 on presentation of proceedings; rule 68 on returning defective petitions), and on e-filing the Electronic Filing Rules assign the same scrutiny to 'the Registry'. In the High Court the office is headed by the Registrar under the Rules of the High Court of Kerala, 1971.
vocabulary.source: Criminal Rules of Practice, Rule 27

vocabulary.gloss: The senior judicial officer who heads the High Court's registry - scrutiny, listing, custody of records and the exercise of delegated administrative and quasi-judicial powers. In a s.138 case the Registrar's office is where a criminal revision or a petition to quash the complaint is presented and scrutinised before it reaches the Bench. The Rules of the High Court of Kerala, 1971 set out the Registrar's powers and duties (Rule 15).
vocabulary.source: Rules of the High Court of Kerala, 1971, Rule 15

vocabulary.gloss: The District Police Chief - the officer who commands the whole police force of a district. A s.138 case rarely involves the police, but the Superintendent heads the district machinery that serves the court's process and executes its warrants. The rank sits in the Kerala Police ladder fixed by s.14 of the Kerala Police Act, 2011; the Police Act, 1861 (s.47) is the older source of the SP's district command.
vocabulary.source: Kerala Police Act, 2011, §14 (police ranks)

vocabulary.gloss: The rank that is the Station House Officer of most police stations - the officer who, in an ordinary criminal case, registers the FIR and investigates, and who in a s.138 case serves the court's summons and executes its warrants. One of the Kerala Police ranks fixed by s.14 of the Kerala Police Act, 2011, with the station-house charge under s.5.
vocabulary.source: Kerala Police Act, 2011, §14 (police ranks)

vocabulary.gloss: The Inspector of Police who heads a circle - a group of police stations - and is the Station House Officer of the larger stations, supervising the Sub-Inspectors under him. In a s.138 case he sits one level above the officer who serves the court's process. A Kerala Police rank fixed by s.14 of the Kerala Police Act, 2011.
vocabulary.source: Kerala Police Act, 2011, §14 (police ranks)

vocabulary.gloss: The apex rank of the police and the head of the whole State force, in whom the administration, supervision and control of the entire Kerala Police is vested, subject to the Government. The role is remote from any single s.138 case but sits at the top of the machinery that serves the courts' process. The State Police Chief is designated under s.18 of the Kerala Police Act, 2011; the rank is the highest in the ladder fixed by s.14.
vocabulary.source: Kerala Police Act, 2011, §18 (State Police Chief)

vocabulary.gloss: The head of a metropolitan Commissionerate - the unitary policing set up for larger cities such as Thiruvananthapuram and Kochi, where the Commissioner combines executive and certain magisterial powers. A s.138 case is tried by a court, not the police, but in a commissionerate city the Commissioner heads the force that serves the court's process. The commissionerate structure is provided for under s.15 of the Kerala Police Act, 2011.
vocabulary.source: Kerala Police Act, 2011, §15 (police structure)

vocabulary.gloss: The basic rank of the police - patrol, guard, beat duty and first response, and often the officer who physically carries and serves the court's process on the ground. Recruited directly through the Kerala PSC; the entrant must meet the eligibility in s.86 of the Kerala Police Act, 2011 and take the oath under s.87, and the rank is the first rung of the ladder fixed by s.14.
vocabulary.source: Kerala Police Act, 2011, §14 (police ranks)

vocabulary.gloss: The oversight body that lays down broad policy for the police and insulates the force from illegitimate pressure. It has no role in any individual s.138 case but is part of the police-accountability structure the domain maps. Constituted under s.24 of the Kerala Police Act, 2011.
vocabulary.source: Kerala Police Act, 2011, §24

vocabulary.gloss: The body that inquires into serious complaints of misconduct against the police, such as custodial wrongdoing or abuse of authority. It does not touch the trial of a s.138 case but is the forum a citizen uses to hold errant officers to account. Constituted under s.110 of the Kerala Police Act, 2011.
vocabulary.source: Kerala Police Act, 2011, §110

institutions.summary: The two institutions a s.138 case runs through on the ground - the police and the courts - with their hierarchy, the people in each role, where each role comes from in law, and how a person enters it. Grounded in the Kerala Police Act, 2011 and the Police Act, 1861 for the police, and the Constitution, the BNSS and the Kerala court rules for the courts.

police.summary: One unified Kerala Police Force. The ranks, in ascending order, are fixed by s.14 of the Kerala Police Act, 2011; the senior ranks are Indian Police Service (IPS) officers, the rest the Kerala Police Service. A s.138 case rarely involves the police (it is a complaint, not an FIR case), but the force is part of the domain.

requirements._about: The normative layer. Everything else in this bundle is descriptive - it says what the law provides. These are statements that BIND a system, each derived from a provision that is named and resolved in `authority`, each with a `test` you can run against a screen, a schema or a workflow. `national` binds every state; a state entry adds only what that state's own instruments require, or where it makes a national requirement stricter (named in `tightens`). The layering is kept rather than flattened, because a rule from central law is stated once.

categories.covers: limitation, cause of action, computation of time
presumptions and the burden of proof

statuses.inferred: a reasonable reading; the reasoning is in `why`
statuses.contested: the authorities divide, and the division is stated
statuses.withdrawn: no longer asserted; the number is never reused

national.title: Normative requirements derived from central law and Supreme Court case law
national.note: Binds every state. A state file adds only what its own instruments require, or tightens one of these. Derived from the central Acts and from Supreme Court case law.

requirements.statement: The system MUST route an appeal against a conviction by a Judicial Magistrate of the first class in a section 138 case to the Court of Session.
requirements.why: A section 138 conviction is by a first class magistrate and carries at most two years, so the appeal lies to the Court of Session and not to the High Court. An appeal filed in the wrong forum is returned, and the time spent is rarely recovered by condonation.

binds.target: appeal - forum for a conviction by a magistrate of the first class

requirements.test: Filing an appeal against a section 138 conviction proposes the Court of Session, and selecting the High Court raises a blocking message naming section 415(3)(a).

requirements.statement: The system MUST NOT permit an order under section 148 directing a deposit of less than twenty per cent of the fine or compensation awarded by the trial court.
requirements.why: Section 148 sets a floor, not a ceiling. An appellate court that orders ten per cent has passed an order below the statutory minimum, and the complainant is deprived of money Parliament intended to reach him while the appeal runs.

authority.heading: Power of Appellate Court to order payment pending appeal against conviction

binds.target: appeal deposit - the twenty per cent floor

requirements.test: With a fine of 500000, a deposit order below 100000 is refused and the message names the floor.

requirements.statement: The system MUST compute the deposit ordered under section 148 on the full fine or compensation awarded by the trial court, without setting off interim compensation already paid.
requirements.why: The proviso says the deposit is in addition to interim compensation paid under section 143A. A build that reuses the section 143A set-off logic for the appellate deposit reduces the deposit by money already paid, which is exactly what the proviso forbids, and it does so silently.

authority.heading: Power of Appellate Court to order payment pending appeal against conviction

binds.target: appeal deposit - no set-off of interim compensation

requirements.test: With interim compensation of 100000 paid and a fine of 500000, the section 148 deposit is computed on 500000, not on 400000.

requirements.statement: The system MUST compute the due date for the section 148 deposit as sixty days from the order, extendable only by a recorded order granting not more than thirty further days on sufficient cause.
requirements.why: The periods mirror section 143A and carry the same risk. A single ninety-day clock gives the appellant an extension he never sought; a bare sixty-day clock reports a lawfully extended deposit as a default, and the appeal is at risk of being taken up as unprosecuted.

authority.heading: Power of Appellate Court to order payment pending appeal against conviction

binds.target: appeal deposit - due date and its extension

requirements.how: Sixty days from the date of the order, or such further period not exceeding thirty days as the court directs on sufficient cause being shown by the appellant.
requirements.test: The deposit due date is sixty days from the order; an extension requires an order capturing the cause and cannot exceed thirty days.

requirements.statement: Where a deposit released to the complainant during the appeal has to be repaid because the appellant is acquitted, the system MUST raise the repayment order with interest at the Reserve Bank of India bank rate prevalent at the beginning of the relevant financial year.
requirements.why: Release of the deposit during the appeal is discretionary but repayment on acquittal is not. Where the acquittal disposal does not raise the repayment, an acquitted appellant is left to recover from the complainant by fresh proceedings money the statute directs be returned within sixty days.

authority.heading: Power of Appellate Court to order payment pending appeal against conviction

binds.target: acquittal on appeal - repayment of a released deposit with interest

requirements.how: With interest at the bank rate published by the Reserve Bank of India prevalent at the beginning of the relevant financial year, within sixty days of the order or such further period not exceeding thirty days as the court directs on sufficient cause shown by the complainant.
requirements.test: Recording an acquittal on an appeal where the deposit was released produces a repayment order stating the principal released, the rate, the financial year and the due date.

requirements.statement: On an appeal against conviction under section 138, the appellate workflow MUST require an express order on the deposit of not less than twenty per cent of the fine or compensation before or with any suspension of sentence.
requirements.why: Surinder Singh Deswal holds that the may in section 148 is ordinarily to be read as shall. Where suspension of sentence can be granted with no deposit decision recorded, the appellate stage becomes a free stay and the convicted drawer holds the money for the years the appeal takes, which is the abuse section 148 was inserted to stop.

authority.cite: NI Act §148 as read in Surinder Singh Deswal v. Virender Gandhi (2019) 11 SCC 341
authority.heading: Power of Appellate Court to order payment pending appeal against conviction

authority.cite: Code of Criminal Procedure §389 as applied in Surinder Singh Deswal v. Virender Gandhi (2019) 11 SCC 341
authority.heading: Suspension of sentence pending the appeal; release of appellant on bail

binds.target: appeal - order on the section 148 deposit

requirements.test: A suspension of sentence order cannot be issued without an accompanying deposit order, whether directing, varying or waiving the deposit.

requirements.statement: The appellate workflow MUST permit the section 148 deposit to be waived, and MUST require reasons where it is.
requirements.why: Jamboo Bhandari holds that the deposit is not an absolute rule and that the appellate court must apply its mind and record reasons where it finds an exceptional case, and further that the court must consider the exception even where the appellant has not asked for it. Both the Sessions Court and the High Court in that case proceeded on the erroneous premise that the deposit admitted of no exception; a system that offers no waiver path builds that same error into every appeal.

authority.cite: NI Act §148 as read in Jamboo Bhandari v. M.P. State Industrial Development Corp Ltd (2023 INSC 822)
authority.heading: Power of Appellate Court to order payment pending appeal against conviction

binds.target: appeal - waiver of the section 148 deposit

requirements.test: The deposit order offers waive as an option; selecting it requires recorded reasons, and the reasons print in the order.

requirements.statement: The system MUST track compliance with a deposit condition attached to a suspension of sentence and MUST support an order vacating the suspension on non-compliance.
requirements.why: Surinder Singh Deswal holds that where suspension was granted on a condition, non-compliance is sufficient for the appellate court to declare the suspension vacated. If the deposit condition is recorded only as narrative in the order and nothing watches the due date, non-payment is invisible, the sentence stays suspended by default, and the condition is worth nothing.

authority.cite: NI Act §148 as read in Surinder Singh Deswal v. Virender Gandhi (2019) 11 SCC 341

authority.heading: Suspension of sentence pending the appeal; release of appellant on bail

binds.target: appeal - deposit compliance monitoring and vacation of suspension

requirements.test: A deposit condition carries a due date and a paid status; expiry without payment raises a task before the appellate court with vacate suspension available.

requirements.statement: The system MUST NOT gate the section 148 appeal deposit on the offence date.
requirements.why: Section 148 and section 143A were inserted by the same amendment, but the Supreme Court has treated them differently: G.J. Raja holds section 143A prospective while Surinder Singh Deswal applies section 148 to appeals even where the cheque predates the amendment, because section 148 creates no new disability and rests on existing recovery machinery. A designer who applies one date rule to both provisions will either refuse a deposit the law requires or impose interim compensation the law forbids.

authority.cite: NI Act §148 as read in Surinder Singh Deswal v. Virender Gandhi (2019) 11 SCC 341
authority.heading: Power of Appellate Court to order payment pending appeal against conviction

authority.cite: NI Act §143A as distinguished in G.J. Raja v. Tejraj Surana (2019) 21 SCC 41
authority.heading: Power to direct interim compensation

binds.target: appeal - applicability of section 148 to pre-amendment offences

requirements.test: An appeal in a case whose cause of action predates 1 September 2018 still requires a section 148 deposit order, while the same case shows interim compensation as unavailable.

requirements.statement: The system MUST treat an offence under section 138 as compoundable at any stage, without reference to the table of compoundable offences in the criminal procedure code.
requirements.why: Section 147 makes every offence under the Negotiable Instruments Act compoundable, notwithstanding the code. Section 138 does not appear in the code's table, so a compounding workflow that reads only the table will refuse compounding in the one class of case where settlement is the normal outcome, and cases that both sides have settled stay on the board.

binds.target: compounding - eligibility of a section 138 offence

requirements.test: Open compounding on a section 138 case at any stage from cognizance to appeal: it is offered, and no message refers to the offence being absent from the table.

requirements.statement: The system MUST record the composition of a section 138 offence as having the effect of an acquittal of the accused, not as a withdrawal or a dismissal.
requirements.why: The code says composition has the effect of an acquittal. Recording it as a withdrawal or a dismissal for non-prosecution changes what the disposal means for the accused, and it changes what a later court or employer reads off the record.

binds.target: disposal - composition recorded as an acquittal

requirements.test: Completing a compounding produces a disposal of acquittal on composition; the disposal list offers no withdrawal outcome for a compounded case.

requirements.statement: Where the accused has been convicted and an appeal is pending, the system MUST NOT allow the composition to be completed without the leave of the court before which the appeal is to be heard.
requirements.why: Composition after conviction requires leave of the appellate court. A build that treats compounding as a purely bilateral act lets a settled matter be closed by the trial court while an appeal is live, leaving a conviction on the record and an appeal with no respondent.

binds.target: compounding after conviction - leave of the appellate court

requirements.test: On a case with a pending appeal, compounding requires an order granting leave to be attached before it can be completed.

requirements.statement: The system MUST NOT refer a section 138 case to a Lok Adalat without recording either the agreement of both parties, or an application by one party with the court's prima facie satisfaction that there are chances of settlement, or the court's own satisfaction that the matter is appropriate.
requirements.why: The Act permits reference only on one of these bases, and in every case except mutual agreement only after a reasonable opportunity of being heard. Bulk referral of section 138 files to a Lok Adalat date without any of this recorded produces references that a party can undo, and the settlement drive loses the very cases it lists.

authority.heading: Cognizance of cases by Lok Adalats.

binds.target: Lok Adalat reference - the recorded basis and the hearing

requirements.how: On the parties' agreement; or on one party's application where the court is prima facie satisfied there are chances of settlement; or on the court's own satisfaction that the matter is appropriate; in the latter two, after giving the parties a reasonable opportunity of being heard.
requirements.test: A reference cannot be created without one of the three bases selected, and selecting either of the last two requires a hearing record.

requirements.statement: The system MUST NOT offer an appeal against an award of a Lok Adalat in a section 138 case.
requirements.why: Every award of a Lok Adalat is deemed a decree and no appeal lies against it. A disposal screen that offers the ordinary appeal route after a Lok Adalat award invites an appeal that no court can entertain, and the parties spend the limitation period discovering it.

binds.target: disposal by Lok Adalat award - available post-disposal actions

requirements.test: After a Lok Adalat award, no appeal action is offered on the case, and the disposal states that the award is final and binding.

requirements.statement: Where a Lok Adalat makes no award because no settlement was reached, the system MUST return the case to the referring court at the stage it had reached before the reference.
requirements.why: The Act says the record goes back and the court proceeds from the stage reached before the reference. A build that resets the case, or that leaves it parked in a referred state, costs the parties the evidence already recorded and the dates already used, and the case restarts for no reason connected to the merits.

authority.heading: Cognizance of cases by Lok Adalats.
Cognizance of cases by Lok Adalats.

binds.target: Lok Adalat reference - return of an unsettled case

requirements.test: Mark a referred case as unsettled: it returns to the referring court showing the same stage, next step and recorded evidence as before the reference.

requirements.statement: Where a section 138 case is settled by a Lok Adalat, the system MUST produce a refund entry for the court fee paid, naming the person entitled to it.
requirements.why: The Act directs that the court fee paid in a case settled by a Lok Adalat be refunded. Where the disposal carries no refund entry, the refund depends on the party knowing to ask and on the office finding the original receipt, which is a discouragement to settlement built into the record.

binds.target: Lok Adalat award - court fee refund entitlement

requirements.test: A settled case produces a refund entry naming the amount and the entitled party, retrievable from the disposal.

requirements.statement: The summons issued to the accused MUST state that he may apply to compound the offence at the first or second hearing and that compounding at that stage carries no costs.
requirements.why: Damodar S. Prabhu directs that the writ of summons be modified to say exactly this, and Indian Bank Association repeats it. The graded costs scheme only works as an incentive if the accused learns of it at the point where the cheap option is still open; a standard criminal summons tells him nothing, and he discovers compounding years later when it costs him a percentage of the cheque.

authority.cite: NI Act §147 as read in Damodar S. Prabhu v. Sayed Babalal H (2010) 5 SCC 663

authority.cite: NI Act §144 as read in Indian Bank Association v. Union of India (2014) 5 SCC 590

authority.cite: NI Act §147 as read in New Win Export v. A. Subramaniam (2024 INSC 535)
authority.heading: Offences to be compoundable

binds.target: summons - compounding notice to the accused

requirements.test: Every generated section 138 summons carries the compounding paragraph; it cannot be suppressed by the issuing officer.

requirements.statement: The system MUST compute compounding costs from the stage of the proceedings at which the cheque amount is paid, on the scale currently in force.
requirements.why: Two scales exist and they differ in both trigger and rate. Damodar S. Prabhu keyed costs to the stage at which the compounding application was made, at ten, fifteen and twenty per cent. Sanjabij Tari revisited and modified those guidelines, keying them to the stage at which the cheque amount is paid, at nil before defence evidence, five per cent after defence evidence but before judgment, seven and a half per cent before the Sessions Court or High Court, and ten per cent before the Supreme Court, with implementation directed by 1 November 2025. The judgment does not say which scale governs an application already pending on that date, so the transition is unsettled. A hardcoded percentage table will be wrong on one side of the change or the other, and the error falls on a party in money.

authority.cite: NI Act §147 as read in Sanjabij Tari v. Kishore S. Borcar (2025 INSC 1158)

authority.cite: NI Act §147 as read in Damodar S. Prabhu v. Sayed Babalal H (2010) 5 SCC 663
authority.heading: Offences to be compoundable

authority.cite: Constitution of India Article 142 as invoked in Damodar S. Prabhu v. Sayed Babalal H (2010) 5 SCC 663
authority.heading: Enforcement of decrees and orders of Supreme Court and orders as to discovery, etc.

binds.target: compounding order - cost scale, effective-dated

requirements.how: Damodar S. Prabhu keyed the costs to the stage at which the compounding application was made, at ten, fifteen and twenty per cent of the cheque amount. Sanjabij Tari modified that scale and keys it to the stage at which the cheque amount is paid: nil before defence evidence; five per cent after defence evidence but before judgment; seven and a half per cent before the Sessions Court or the High Court; ten per cent before the Supreme Court. Whichever scale is applied, the costs are computed on the amount of the cheque.
requirements.test: The scale in force is held as effective-dated data with its source judgment, so changing it is a data change and not a release; a compounding order names the scale version applied, and an order made across the transition date records on its face which scale was chosen and why.

requirements.statement: Compounding costs MUST be routed to the Legal Services Authority operating at the level of the court before which compounding takes place.
requirements.why: Damodar S. Prabhu is explicit that costs go to the District Legal Services Authority for a Magistrate or Sessions Court, the State Authority for the High Court and the National Authority for the Supreme Court, and Sanjabij Tari keeps the same destination. A payment step that treats the costs as a court fee or as money payable to the complainant sends the deposit to the wrong account and the compounding order cannot be complied with.

authority.cite: NI Act §147 as read in Damodar S. Prabhu v. Sayed Babalal H (2010) 5 SCC 663
authority.heading: Offences to be compoundable

authority.cite: Legal Services Authorities Act §19 as read in Damodar S. Prabhu v. Sayed Babalal H (2010) 5 SCC 663
authority.heading: Organisation of Lok Adalats.

binds.target: compounding - deposit of costs with the Legal Services Authority at the level of the court

requirements.test: The payee of the compounding costs is derived from the court's level and cannot be edited to the complainant or to the court's own fee head.

requirements.statement: The system MUST record the complainant's consent as a condition of any compounding order made by a trial or appellate court.
requirements.why: JIK Industries holds that section 147 makes the offence compoundable but does not displace the requirement of the aggrieved party's consent. The authorities beyond that point divide. Meters and Instruments held that a court could close proceedings without consent once the complainant was compensated, and was disapproved by the Constitution Bench on the section 258 route it used. Raj Reddy Kallem allows a conviction to be set aside on compensation without consent, but expressly as a quashing under Article 142 rather than a compounding, and that power is not available to a trial court. A workflow that lets a magistrate compound without recorded consent is relying on the one line of authority that has been cut back.

authority.cite: NI Act §147 as read in JIK Industries Ltd v. Amarlal V. Jumani (2012) 3 SCC 255
authority.heading: Offences to be compoundable

authority.cite: Constitution of India Article 142 as applied in Raj Reddy Kallem v. State of Haryana (2024 SCC OnLine SC 3223)

authority.cite: BNSS §359 as read in Damodar S. Prabhu v. Sayed Babalal H (2010) 5 SCC 663
authority.heading: Compounding of offences

binds.target: compounding order - recorded consent of the complainant

requirements.test: A compounding order cannot be made without a recorded consent from the complainant or the complainant's authorised representative; a disposal on payment without consent is available only as a distinct mode marked as an Article 142 order of the Supreme Court.

requirements.statement: The system MUST provide a court-operated online payment channel for the cheque amount at the district level, and the summons MUST carry the link or code for it.
requirements.why: Sanjabij Tari directs each Principal District and Sessions Judge to create and operationalise dedicated secure QR or UPI payment facilities, and directs that the summons expressly mention the accused's option to pay the cheque amount at the initial stage through that link. Where the accused who is willing to pay has no channel except a bank draft tendered in court on a hearing date, the payment happens at the pace of the cause list and the case is not settled at the threshold.

authority.cite: NI Act §147 as read in Sanjabij Tari v. Kishore S. Borcar (2025 INSC 1158)
authority.heading: Offences to be compoundable

authority.cite: NI Act §144 as read in Sanjabij Tari v. Kishore S. Borcar (2025 INSC 1158)
authority.heading: Mode of service of summons

binds.target: early payment - district online payment channel referenced in the summons

requirements.test: The summons carries a working payment reference; a payment against it is attributed to the case, notified to the complainant, and raises the compounding or closure decision before the court.

requirements.statement: Where the accused tenders the cheque amount but the complainant demands more, the system MAY offer the court a plea-of-guilty and sentencing route in place of compounding.
requirements.why: Sanjabij Tari directs that if the complainant asks for payment beyond the cheque amount or settlement of the entire loan, the magistrate may suggest that the accused plead guilty and may exercise the powers under section 255(2) or 255(3) CrPC or section 278 BNSS, or extend the benefit of the Probation of Offenders Act. Without that branch the case has nowhere to go: consent is withheld, compounding fails, and a matter in which the money is on the table is set down for full trial.

authority.cite: Code of Criminal Procedure §255 as read in Sanjabij Tari v. Kishore S. Borcar (2025 INSC 1158)

authority.cite: BNSS §278 as read in Sanjabij Tari v. Kishore S. Borcar (2025 INSC 1158)
authority.heading: Acquittal or conviction

binds.target: settlement failure - plea of guilty and sentencing branch

requirements.test: Where a tender of the cheque amount is recorded and consent is refused, the court is offered the plea-and-sentence branch alongside continue trial, and the tender remains on the record.

requirements.statement: Where a supervision order is made on releasing an offender on probation, the system MUST furnish a copy to the offender, to each surety and to the probation officer named in the order.
requirements.why: The Act names all three recipients and requires the copy to be furnished forthwith, because the order imposes conditions each of them has to observe or enforce. A supervision order that exists only on the court file cannot be complied with by a surety who has never seen its conditions.

authority.heading: Power of court to release certain offenders on probation of good conduct
Power of court to release certain offenders on probation of good conduct

binds.target: supervision order - copies to offender, sureties and probation officer

requirements.how: One copy of the supervision order to each of the offender, the sureties, if any, and the probation officer concerned.
requirements.test: Making a supervision order generates three addressed copies and records their delivery; the order cannot be closed with a recipient unserved.

requirements.statement: The system MUST supply public documents of the court in accessible formats.
requirements.why: Section 12(4)(a) directs the appropriate Government to take steps to ensure that its public documents are in accessible formats; it does not in terms bind the court's copying channel, so applying it to the copies a court supplies is a reading of the access-to-justice duty in section 12(1). The failure it prevents is concrete: a judgment or order supplied only as a scanned image is unreadable to a blind party in a section 138 case, so the copy the court supplies does not in fact tell that party what was decided.

authority.heading: Access to justice.

binds.target: copies of orders and judgments - accessible format

requirements.test: A copy supplied through the portal carries a text layer or a structured text alternative, and a screen reader can read the operative part.

requirements.statement: The system MUST supply a copy of the judgment to the convicted accused free of cost, immediately on pronouncement where the sentence includes imprisonment and on his application in every case in which the judgment is appealable by him.
requirements.why: The commonest section 138 outcome is fine and compensation with no imprisonment, so the automatic copy is not engaged and the copy comes instead on application. A drawer who does not know he must ask holds no copy of the judgment his appeal has to be accompanied by, and the appeal period runs while he waits. A build that issues the copy only where imprisonment was awarded follows the letter of one sub-section and defeats the appeal right the next sub-section protects.

authority.heading: Copy of judgment to be given to accused and other persons
Copy of judgment to be given to accused and other persons
Copy of judgment to be given to the accused and other persons

binds.target: judgment - copy to the convicted accused

requirements.how: On a sentence of imprisonment, a copy immediately after pronouncement, free of cost and without application. Otherwise, on the application of the accused, a certified copy without delay and free of cost wherever the judgment is appealable by him, with a translation in his own language if practicable or in the language of the court where he so desires.
requirements.test: A conviction with imprisonment issues the copy with no application recorded; a fine-only conviction raises a prompt to the accused or his advocate to apply, and the copy issues free of cost with no fee entry.

requirements.statement: The system MUST allow the complainant's evidence to be filed as an affidavit and to be read in evidence in the enquiry or trial without a separate examination-in-chief.
requirements.why: Section 145 is what makes a section 138 trial capable of being finished in a handful of hearings. Where the system models evidence only as deposition recorded in court, every complainant must attend and be examined, and the six-month target in section 143(3) becomes unreachable in any court with a normal docket.

binds.target: evidence - complainant's affidavit as examination-in-chief

requirements.test: An affidavit filed by the complainant appears in the evidence record as examination-in-chief and the case can move to cross-examination without a deposition being recorded.

requirements.statement: The system MUST issue a summons to a person who has given evidence on affidavit on the application of the prosecution or the accused, without offering the court a decision to allow or refuse that application.
requirements.why: Section 145(2) says the court may summon on its own view but shall summon on the application of a party. If the workflow models the summoning of the deponent as a discretionary judicial action, an accused who applies for cross-examination can be refused, and the conviction that follows rests on untested affidavit evidence.

binds.target: evidence - application to cross-examine a deponent on affidavit

requirements.test: An application by the accused to summon the affidavit deponent produces a summons; the workflow offers no allow or refuse decision on a party's application, only on the court's own motion.

requirements.statement: The system MUST store the bank's slip or memo of dishonour as an image or document showing the official mark, not only the reason for return as a coded value.
requirements.why: The statutory presumption of dishonour attaches to production of the slip or memo having the official mark on it. A record holding only a return reason code has nothing to produce, so the complainant must call a bank officer to prove a fact the statute presumes.

authority.heading: Bank’s slip prima facie evidence of certain facts

binds.target: dishonour record - the bank memo document bearing the official mark

requirements.test: The dishonour record cannot be saved on a reason code alone; the memo document is required and is retrievable as an exhibit.

requirements.statement: Where an entry in a banker's book is relied on, the system MUST hold the certificate that accompanies the certified copy, in the form the Bankers' Books Evidence Act prescribes.
requirements.why: A copy of a bank statement is not evidence; a certified copy with the statutory certificate is. Where the certificate is missing or is signed by someone other than the principal accountant or branch manager, the entry is inadmissible, and the complainant discovers this when the account statement is tendered.

authority.heading: Mode of proof of entries in bankers’ books

binds.target: bank statement exhibit - the accompanying statutory certificate

requirements.how: A certificate at the foot of the copy that it is a true copy of the entry, that the entry is in one of the ordinary books of the bank and was made in the usual and ordinary course of business, and that the book is still in the bank's custody, dated and subscribed by the principal accountant or manager with name and official title; for a printout, the further certificates required for computer-held records.
requirements.test: A banker's book entry cannot be marked as an exhibit without the certificate attached, and the certificate capture records the name and official title of the signatory.

requirements.statement: Where an electronic record such as a cheque truncation image or an electronic bank record is tendered, the system MUST require the statutory certificate to accompany it on each occasion it is submitted for admission.
requirements.why: The certificate is the condition of admissibility of the computer output, and the Adhiniyam requires it at each instance the record is submitted. Where the system attaches the certificate once at upload and never again, later tenders of the same image go in uncertified, and the entire electronic proof of dishonour is open to challenge.

authority.heading: Admissibility of electronic records. –– (1) Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act,

binds.target: electronic exhibit - certificate required at each submission for admission

requirements.how: A certificate identifying the electronic record and the manner of its production, giving particulars of the device, and dealing with the conditions in section 63(2), signed by the person in charge of the computer or communication device or of the management of the relevant activities and by an expert, in the form set out in the Schedule.
requirements.test: Tender the same truncated cheque image at two hearings: the system requires a certificate at each tender and records both.

requirements.statement: The system MUST record, for every witness, whether an oath or a solemn affirmation was administered before the witness deposed.
requirements.why: Oath or affirmation is required of every witness, and a witness who objects to being sworn is entitled to affirm instead. Recording only that the witness was sworn erases the choice, which matters to the witness, and leaves the record unable to show what was in fact administered.

authority.heading: Oaths or affirmations to be made by witnesses, interpreters and jurors.
Affirmation by persons desiring to affirm.

binds.target: deposition - oath or affirmation, as an explicit value

requirements.test: The deposition header carries an enumerated value of oath or affirmation; there is no single sworn checkbox.

requirements.statement: Where a witness deposes through an interpreter, the system MUST record the interpreter's identity and that the interpreter was sworn or affirmed.
requirements.why: The Oaths Act puts the interpreter of a witness's evidence under the same obligation as the witness. In a section 138 trial the interpreter is often arranged on the day and never named in the record, so a later dispute about what the witness actually said has no one to answer it.

authority.heading: Oaths or affirmations to be made by witnesses, interpreters and jurors.

binds.target: deposition - interpreter identity and oath

requirements.test: Marking a deposition as interpreted requires the interpreter's name and the oath or affirmation record before the deposition can be closed.

requirements.statement: The system MUST NOT treat a missing or irregular oath entry as invalidating a deposition or as a ground to reject it from the record.
requirements.why: The Oaths Act says in terms that no omission to take an oath and no irregularity in administering it invalidates the proceeding or renders the evidence inadmissible. A validation rule that voids or blocks a deposition for a missing oath field creates a defect the law expressly refuses to create, and does so silently in every court that uses the build.

authority.heading: Proceedings and evidence not invalidated by omission of oath or irregularity.

binds.target: deposition - handling of a missing oath entry

requirements.test: Save a deposition with the oath field empty: the record is retained with the gap visible as a warning, and the deposition is neither voided nor excluded from the evidence list.

requirements.statement: The system MUST NOT put the accused in a section 138 case on oath unless the accused is being examined as a witness for the defence.
requirements.why: The Oaths Act forbids administering an oath to the accused in a criminal proceeding except where he offers himself as a defence witness. A generic hearing screen that swears everyone who speaks turns the accused's statement into sworn testimony and touches the protection against self-incrimination.

authority.heading: Oaths or affirmations to be made by witnesses, interpreters and jurors.
Protection in respect of conviction for offences.

binds.target: hearing - oath administration for the accused

requirements.test: The oath action is unavailable against a person recorded as the accused unless that person has been entered as a defence witness.

requirements.statement: The system MUST require an affidavit tendered in a judicial proceeding to be sworn before a court, judge, magistrate or other person empowered by the High Court to administer oaths for that purpose.
requirements.why: The Oaths Act empowers different classes of persons for judicial-proceeding affidavits and for other affidavits. An affidavit under section 145 sworn before someone empowered only for general affidavits is defective, and the complainant's entire examination-in-chief goes with it.

binds.target: affidavit - the attesting authority and the power under which it was sworn

requirements.test: An affidavit record captures the attesting authority and the class of empowerment, and an affidavit attested by an authority empowered only for non-judicial affidavits is flagged.

requirements.statement: The system MUST allow the defence that the cheque was delivered blank or incomplete to be recorded as a distinct issue on the case, with the extent said to have been filled in later.
requirements.why: A signed blank cheque carries a prima facie authority to complete it, but only up to the amount the stamp covers and only in favour of a holder in due course to the full extent. Where the case record cannot distinguish this defence from a bare denial of the debt, the finding does not address it and the judgment is silent on the point actually argued. Section 20 states the substantive rule; treating it as a recordable issue is the reading that makes it checkable.

binds.target: defence - inchoate instrument as an enumerated ground

requirements.test: The defence grounds list includes delivery of a blank or incomplete instrument, and selecting it opens fields for what is alleged to have been filled in and by whom.

requirements.statement: The system MUST allow an alleged material alteration of the cheque to be recorded as a distinct issue, with a field for whether the party alleged to be bound consented to it.
requirements.why: Material alteration renders the instrument void against a party who did not consent, unless the alteration carried out the common intention. That turns on consent, which is a fact someone has to plead and the court has to find. A record with no place for it produces judgments that deal with the alteration and never with the consent. Section 87 states the rule; recording consent as a distinct fact is the reading of it.

binds.target: defence - material alteration and consent to it

requirements.test: Selecting material alteration as a defence opens a consent field, and the judgment template requires a finding on both the alteration and the consent.

requirements.statement: Where the cheque is one in the electronic form, the system MUST record whether it was signed with a digital signature or an electronic signature in a secure system.
requirements.why: The presumption that a secure electronic signature was affixed with intent, and that a secure record has not been altered, applies only to secure records and signatures. A system that stores an electronic cheque without recording its signature type cannot tell the court whether the presumption is available, and the complainant must prove by evidence what he could have had presumed.

authority.heading: Presumption as to electronic records and electronic signatures

binds.target: electronic cheque - signature type and secure status

requirements.test: An electronic cheque record carries an enumerated signature type; the case view states whether the section 86 presumption is available and why.

requirements.statement: The system MUST allow the complainant's affidavit filed with the complaint to be read as evidence at both the pre-summoning and the post-summoning stages, without a second examination.
requirements.why: Indian Bank Association holds that the affidavit and documents filed with the complaint are good enough at both stages and that there is no necessity to recall and re-examine the complainant after summoning unless the magistrate passes a specific order. A workflow that requires a fresh examination-in-chief after appearance adds a hearing to every case for no evidentiary gain and defeats the six month endeavour.

authority.heading: Evidence on affidavit

binds.target: trial - complainant's evidence after appearance of the accused

requirements.test: After the accused appears, the complainant's affidavit already on record is marked as evidence without a new filing; a recall step exists but is not on the default path.

requirements.statement: The system MUST NOT offer the accused evidence on affidavit as a matter of right.
requirements.why: Mandvi Cooperative Bank holds that section 145(1) provides for the complainant's evidence on affidavit and that the court cannot read the accused into it, and it set aside a High Court direction that allowed the accused to tender evidence on affidavit on request. A defence-evidence screen that offers file affidavit alongside lead oral evidence puts the court in breach of that holding, and the resulting evidence is liable to be excluded.

authority.cite: NI Act §145(1) as read in Mandvi Cooperative Bank Ltd v. Nimesh B. Thakore (2010) 3 SCC 83
authority.heading: Evidence on affidavit

binds.target: defence evidence - mode of recording

requirements.test: The defence evidence step offers oral examination as the mode; affidavit evidence for the accused is available only under a recorded order of the court, not as a self-service option.

requirements.statement: The system MUST record recall of a deponent for cross-examination as an order made on an application under section 145(2) or on the court's own recorded reasons.
requirements.why: Indian Bank Association holds that a complainant is recalled only where the magistrate passes a specific order saying why, on an application by the accused or suo motu under section 145(2). Where recall is a routine listing action with no application and no reasons, the summary trial reverts in practice to a full trial, which is exactly the drift the direction was issued to stop.

binds.target: trial - recall of a deponent for cross-examination

requirements.test: Recall cannot be scheduled without either a linked section 145(2) application or a recorded reason; both appear in the order sheet.

requirements.statement: The system MUST record the custody of the original cheque and the original return memo, distinctly from any scanned or e-filed image of them.
requirements.why: The cheque is the instrument on which the offence rests and the document itself produced for the inspection of the court is the primary evidence of it; a scan is secondary evidence and admissible only on the conditions the Adhiniyam imposes. Electronic filing makes it easy for the original never to reach the court at all, and the point is taken at the stage of marking exhibits, after the complainant's evidence is closed. A record that holds only the image cannot tell the court whether the original exists, where it is, or who holds it.

binds.target: exhibit - custody of the original instrument, distinct from its image

requirements.test: The cheque record carries a custody value naming who holds the original and where, populated independently of the uploaded image; marking the cheque as an exhibit is blocked while custody is unrecorded.

requirements.statement: The system MUST require the section 138 complaint to exist as a written complaint document before it can be numbered.
requirements.why: Section 142 permits cognizance only upon a complaint in writing. A filing flow that captures structured fields and generates nothing signed leaves the court with no complaint to take cognizance of, and the defect goes to jurisdiction rather than to form.

binds.target: complaint filing - a written complaint document as a precondition to numbering

requirements.test: Attempt to number a case from form fields alone with no complaint document attached: the build refuses and names section 142(1)(a).

requirements.statement: The system MUST record the capacity in which the complainant sues, as payee or as holder in due course, as a distinct field on the complaint.
requirements.why: Only the payee or the holder in due course can set a section 138 prosecution going. Where the complainant is an indorsee or an assignee, the capacity determines whether the complaint is competent at all, and it determines which presumptions the complainant can call on. A free-text party record cannot be queried for it and cannot be validated.

binds.target: complainant - capacity as payee or holder in due course

requirements.test: The complainant record carries an enumerated capacity field; it is mandatory; the complaint cannot be numbered without it.

requirements.statement: The system MUST record the payment of process fees before any summons or warrant can be issued in the case.
requirements.why: Process cannot issue until the fees payable are paid, and if they are not paid within a reasonable time the complaint may be dismissed. A workflow that issues summons on the magistrate's order without checking the fee produces process the court had no power to issue, and a workflow with no fee clock cannot tell the magistrate which files are ripe for dismissal.

binds.target: issue of process - fee payment as a precondition

requirements.test: With process fee unpaid, the issue-summons action is unavailable and the case appears in a list of complaints awaiting process fee with the elapsed time shown.

requirements.statement: The system MUST allow either party to claim free legal services on one of the statutory criteria, at any stage of a section 138 case.
requirements.why: Entitlement to legal services turns on categories the court sees at filing, such as a woman, a member of a Scheduled Caste or Tribe, a person with disability, or income below the prescribed limit. If the filing flow has nowhere to record the claim, an entitled accused in a section 138 case appears unrepresented and the entitlement is discovered, if at all, at the stage of sentence.

binds.target: filing and appearance - claim to free legal services

requirements.test: A claim can be attached to either party from the filing screen and from any later hearing screen; the ground is chosen from an enumerated list drawn from section 12, free text is not accepted as a ground, and the claim is visible on the case record to the court and to the legal services authority.

requirements.statement: Where the claim to free legal services rests on income, the system MUST accept an affidavit of income as sufficient proof of means.
requirements.why: The Act says an affidavit as to income may be regarded as sufficient unless the authority has reason to disbelieve it. A build that demands an income certificate from a revenue authority substitutes a document the statute does not require, and the indigent accused in a section 138 case goes unrepresented for the weeks it takes to obtain one.

binds.target: claim to legal services - proof of means

requirements.how: An affidavit made by the person as to income may be regarded as sufficient unless the concerned authority has reason to disbelieve it.
requirements.test: An income-based claim can be completed with an affidavit alone; no revenue-issued certificate is required as a precondition.

requirements.statement: The system MUST make the filing registry able to accept and store documents in accessible formats where a party is a person with disability.
requirements.why: The access-to-justice duty requires filing departments and registries to be equipped to file, store and refer to documents and evidence in accessible formats. A portal that accepts only scanned image PDFs makes the record unreadable to a blind complainant or accused, and the barrier is created by the system rather than removed by it.

authority.heading: Access to justice.

binds.target: filing registry - acceptance and storage of documents in accessible formats

requirements.test: A text-layer PDF or tagged document can be filed and is retrievable in that form; the registry does not flatten filings into images without a text layer.

requirements.statement: The system MUST require a sworn affidavit with the complaint disclosing whether any other complaint on the same transaction is pending in any other court.
requirements.why: Damodar S. Prabhu made this disclosure mandatory to stop the same transaction being litigated across several jurisdictions. Where the affidavit is optional or is collected as free text, the registry has nothing to match on, multiplicity is discovered only when an accused raises it, and the cost order the Court contemplated cannot be made.

authority.cite: NI Act §142 as read in Damodar S. Prabhu v. Sayed Babalal H (2010) 5 SCC 663
authority.heading: Cognizance of offences

binds.target: filing - mandatory no-other-complaint affidavit

requirements.test: A complaint cannot be accepted without the affidavit; the answer is stored as a structured yes/no with court and case particulars where yes, not as prose.

requirements.statement: Every complaint under section 138 MUST carry the prescribed synopsis, placed immediately after the index and before the complaint itself.
requirements.why: Sanjabij Tari prescribes the exact synopsis format and directs High Courts and District Courts to implement it. Its whole purpose is that the magistrate can verify the ingredients and limitation from one page instead of reconstructing them from the body of the complaint. A system that generates a complaint without it produces a document courts are directed to expect and do not get, and scrutiny stays as slow as it was.

authority.cite: NI Act §142 as read in Sanjabij Tari v. Kishore S. Borcar (2025 INSC 1158)

authority.cite: NI Act §138 as read in Sanjabij Tari v. Kishore S. Borcar (2025 INSC 1158)
authority.heading: Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in the account

binds.target: complaint - prescribed synopsis sheet

requirements.how: The synopsis carries seven heads in order: particulars of the parties (for a company or firm accused, the registered address, the managing director or partner, the signatory and the persons vicariously liable); cheque details (number, date, amount, drawee bank and branch, account number); dishonour (date of presentation, date of return memo, branch where dishonoured, reason); statutory notice (date, mode of service, date of despatch and tracking number, proof and date of delivery, whether served and if not the reasons, reply if any); cause of action (date of accrual, jurisdiction invoked under section 142(2), whether any other section 138 complaint is pending between the same parties and if so the court, date and year); relief sought (summoning and trial, and whether interim compensation under section 143A is sought); and filed through complainant or authorised representative.
requirements.test: The generated complaint bundle opens with a synopsis containing all seven heads; every field is populated from structured data, not typed prose, and any field left blank is reported at scrutiny.

requirements.statement: The system MUST present a complaint for scrutiny to the magistrate on the day it is filed, and MUST allow cognizance and issue of summons in that same step where the affidavit and documents are in order.
requirements.why: The first direction in Indian Bank Association is that on the day the complaint is presented the magistrate scrutinises it and, if the affidavit and documents are in order, takes cognizance and directs summons. Where a system routes filing to a registry queue that reaches the magistrate weeks later, the six month endeavour under section 143(3) is lost before the case has begun.

authority.cite: NI Act §145 as read in Indian Bank Association v. Union of India (2014) 5 SCC 590
authority.heading: Evidence on affidavit

binds.target: filing to cognizance - same-day scrutiny

requirements.how: Scrutiny, cognizance and the direction to issue summons are a single magistrate action on the filing date; the complainant's affidavit and documents are the material examined, with no separate preliminary evidence step.
requirements.test: The interval between the filing timestamp and the scrutiny listing is zero days by default, and the cognizance action offers issue summons without an intervening step.

requirements.statement: Where the payee is a company, firm or other juristic person, the system MUST record that entity as the complainant and separately identify the authorised natural person who presents and prosecutes the complaint.
requirements.why: Section 142 requires the complaint to be made by the payee, and a juristic payee can act only through a person. TRL Krosaki holds that the company is the de jure complainant and its authorised employee the de facto complainant, and that the latter may change over the life of the case. A schema with a single complainant field forces the drafter to choose, and either the complaint is not in the name of the payee, which is the only eligibility condition section 142 imposes, or the human being who must be examined is nowhere on the record.

authority.cite: NI Act §142(1)(a) as read in TRL Krosaki Refractories Ltd v. SMS Asia Pvt Ltd (2022) 7 SCC 612
authority.heading: Cognizance of offences

binds.target: complaint - complainant entity and its authorised representative as distinct parties

requirements.test: Selecting a juristic complainant makes the representative record mandatory, with name, designation and the authorisation document; replacing the representative does not alter the complainant of record.

requirements.statement: Where the complaint is filed through a power-of-attorney holder or an authorised representative, it MUST carry an explicit averment of that person's personal knowledge of the transaction.
requirements.why: A.C. Narayanan requires the assertion of the attorney holder's knowledge to be made explicitly in the complaint, and holds that an attorney holder without knowledge cannot be examined as a witness. If the complaint form does not compel that averment, the complainant's own evidence becomes inadmissible mid-trial and the prosecution collapses on a defect that could have been cured at filing.

authority.heading: Cognizance of offences

binds.target: complaint - knowledge averment where filed through a representative

requirements.test: Selecting filed through representative makes the knowledge averment a required field, and the averment appears verbatim in the generated complaint.

requirements.statement: The system MUST hold the instrument of authority relied on by a representative complainant, and MUST record whether it expressly permits sub-delegation.
requirements.why: A.C. Narayanan holds that a power of attorney holder can further delegate only where the instrument expressly says so, and that sub-delegation otherwise is invalid in law. Where the record holds only the name of the person signing, an invalid sub-delegation is invisible until the accused produces the deed at trial and the complaint is found to have been instituted by someone with no authority.

authority.cite: NI Act §142 as read in A.C. Narayanan v. State of Maharashtra (2014) 11 SCC 790

binds.target: complaint - instrument of authority and its sub-delegation clause

requirements.test: The representative record links to an uploaded authority document with a sub-delegation permitted yes/no; a representative appointed by sub-delegation cannot be recorded where the answer is no.

requirements.statement: The system MUST NOT block filing or cognizance for want of proof of the representative's authorisation or knowledge.
requirements.why: TRL Krosaki holds that an averment of authorisation and knowledge with prima facie material is enough for cognizance, that dismissal at the threshold on the authorisation question is not justified, and that a genuine dispute about it is an issue for trial. A scrutiny rule that demands documentary proof at the counter converts a triable issue into a filing bar and sends the complainant to the High Court.

binds.target: scrutiny - authorisation of the representative complainant

requirements.test: A complaint carrying the averment but no supporting resolution is accepted and numbered; the absence is recorded as an issue for trial, not as a scrutiny defect.

requirements.statement: Where the drawer of the cheque is a company or a firm, the system MUST require that entity to be arraigned as an accused before any director, partner or signatory can be arraigned.
requirements.why: Aneeta Hada holds that for vicarious liability under section 141 the company must be an accused, and Dilip Hariramani applies the same rule to a firm, setting aside a partner's conviction because the firm was not prosecuted. A complaint form that permits a director to be named alone produces a prosecution that is void from the outset, and the defect is discovered on appeal after a conviction.
